We create the South American (It's like America, only SOUTH") campsite of Russell, Kevin (Kevin's a girl?) hiding in the bushes, and of course "It's a talking dog!" Doug. We now have adults bringing THEIR kids, telling us ours was always their favorite house and they are so glad to be able to bring their kids now. Hell yes we cry every time.I will do this until my body won't let me, and then I will hire people to set it up so I can still come greet the kids.

@[user]​​⁠i think part of it for me is just pure spite. spite against the lies i've been fed in my head that want to keep me insecure and miserable. spite against the idea that i deserved anything that happened to me. spite against the idea i can't enjoy new things the way a child would now that i'm in my 20s. 
i think part of what makes seeing the kids live their lives cathartic is that i allow myself to feel the same joy and wonder as them. because i grew up underprivileged, often when they do things for the first time, it's the first time for me as well. it was a bit hard navigating to adulthood as i got older because i felt like i missed out developmentally, but being around children gives me the experience of getting to experience those things with other people who are just has happy to be doing them. 
i grew up poor, i was bullied at school, and i was abused by my family but still managed to have quite a strong spirit beneath all of the layers of trauma. i think something in me just knew life wasn't supposed to feel like it did. when i was 18 i moved to australia (i grew up in iowa and had never taken a plane, or even seen the ocean before then lmao) and haven't looked back since. i'm 23 now and the life i've lived now is beyond my wildest dreams. i'm sure to some it's not impressive but i've gone to so many places around the world and had so many great experiences that sometimes it's hard to believe i used to be the "weird poor girl" at school who got picked on and lived in a section 8 apartment.
